Designing a robust voice parser for your gym logger

The key design decision is this: don't treat speech recognition output as clean text. Treat it as a noisy observation of a structured command. Your parser should reconstruct the most likely workout entry from the transcript, its alternatives, and the grammar of gym logging—while preserving uncertainty instead of silently inventing numbers.

For your plain-JavaScript app, I'd build a small, deterministic pipeline rather than a general-purpose NLP system or an LLM dependency.

The most important principle is to separate three things:

  1. What Chrome recognized — raw transcript and alternatives.

  2. What the speaker probably said — normalized, structured interpretation with confidence.

  3. What the app commits — only after the interpretation is sufficiently reliable, with an easy way to correct it.

Your examples reveal that most recognition errors are systematic. They can be handled with domain-specific rules, but the rules must be context-aware: grapes is probably reps after a set count, whereas 20 grapes in an unrelated conversation should not automatically become 20 reps.

1. Recommended architecture

A. Web Speech API

Final transcript + up to 2 alternatives

B. Candidate selection

Compare all three hypotheses; retain their provenance

C. Domain-aware normalization

Reps variants, kg/lb variants, spoken numbers, ASR insertions

D. Workout grammar parser

Set boundaries, weights, reps, warm-ups, assistance, notes, comments

E. Validation + confidence

Check competing interpretations and flag ambiguous fields

F. Preview and commit

Confirm when needed; don't lose the original transcript

Why this order matters: if you globally replace every occurrence of 4 with for, or every 20th with 20, you will introduce errors that are harder to detect later. Instead, normalization should propose interpretations, and the workout grammar should decide which ones make sense.

2. Normalize the errors that actually occur in your logs

Don't build a single giant replacement list. Use contextual rewrite rules that run only where a gym command makes the rewrite plausible.

A. Reps: the highest-value correction

Your observed vocabulary is unusually consistent: raps, rips, ribs, wraps, rapes, grapes, tips, apps, and sometimes g all appear where reps are expected.

I'd use these tiers:

Recognized text

Proposed interpretation

When to apply

raps, rips, ribs, rapes, wraps

reps

Near a plausible rep count or set phrase

grapes

reps

After a number in a workout-set context

tips

reps

Especially in a fragment like 20 tips for

apps

reps

After a plausible rep count, especially after for

g

reps

Only in a strongly supported pattern such as for 20 g

ra, rap

incomplete reps

Interim display only; do not finalize

A key distinction: the first five are plausible word-level substitutions. g is a much more aggressive inference because it could be a real unit, an abbreviation, or the tail of a different recognition error. Only allow that inference when the surrounding structure strongly supports it.

For example:

  • 20 kgs for 10 grapes → 20 kg × 10 reps.

  • 20 tips for → an incomplete command with a likely rep-related token, not a completed set.

  • 20 kgs for 10 grapes then 5 kgs for two reps → two complete sets.

  • 20 kgs warm UPS → a warm-up command, not 20 reps.

B. Weight units: handle kg is and lb is

The recognizer appears to split spoken plural units into multiple tokens:

Raw transcript

Canonical interpretation

20 kgs

20 kg

20 kg is

20 kg when followed by a valid set continuation

30 lb is

30 lb when used as a weight declaration

5 kgs for

5 kg for — preserve the unfinished continuation

Don't blindly remove every is. It may be genuine speech, and it may separate a number from a later quantity.

A practical rule is to treat kg, kgs, kilogram, kilograms, lb, lbs, pound, and pounds as unit aliases, then optionally consume an immediately following is as a recognition artifact when the surrounding tokens support that interpretation.

Keep the canonical units distinct:

  • kg → kilograms

  • lb → pounds

  • pin / block → machine setting, not a mass unit

This distinction matters because a machine setting of 5 cannot be converted to kilograms without equipment-specific information.

C. Numbers: repair the structure, not every number word

The examples demonstrate three different errors that should not share one global rule.

420 → for 20

Only consider this when it appears after a weight and a preceding set, where a new rep count is expected.

to enter apps → twenty reps

A phrase-level correction, justified when a weight has just been declared and a rep count is missing.

20th → 20

Accept a spoken-number interpretation when the grammar expects a quantity, but don't globally remove ordinal suffixes from all text.

I'd prioritize the rules in this order:

  1. Parse clearly recognized numbers and unit expressions.

  2. Repair known number-word substitutions in expected quantity positions.

  3. Resolve for versus four from the surrounding grammar.

  4. Reject or flag a rewrite when two valid interpretations remain.

The important case is 5 kg is 4 12. The intended interpretation may be 5 kg for 12 reps, with 4 being a misrecognized for. But the string alone does not prove that. Your parser should use the fact that a weight has been declared and a rep count is expected, not a universal rule that every 4 means for.

Also, don't impose a universal maximum rep count of 20. Your actual logs include 40 reps. A value can be unusual without being invalid.

3. Use a small grammar with explicit set boundaries

I recommend parsing the utterance into a sequence of set candidates, then interpreting each candidate independently.

Your grammar can start with these conceptual patterns:

Plain text
COMMAND := SET (SET_SEPARATOR SET)* COMMENT? SET_SEPARATOR := "then" | "drop set" | "drop to" | "dropped to" | "dropped" SET := WEIGHT [WARMUP] [CONNECTOR REP_COUNT REP_WORD] [SET_FLAGS] [SUPPORT] [QUICK_NOTES]

This is a starting grammar, not a literal regex that covers every possible ordering. Real speech will vary, and you may hear the count before the unit or omit a connector entirely.

For your app, use a two-stage parser:

  • Stage 1: segmentation. Find explicit separators and command boundaries.

  • Stage 2: interpretation. Parse weight, reps, flags, support, and notes within each segment.

Keep add comment, comment, and note as explicit command boundaries. Once one is detected, parse the remaining text as a comment instead of continuing to interpret its words as sets.

Example: the complete command

Input:

60 lbs for 10 reps then 30 lbs for 12 reps add comment slow and heavy

Expected output:

Set 1

60 lb × 10 reps

Set 2 · Drop set

30 lb × 12 reps

Comment

Slow and heavy

The second set is not a new independent command. It's another set in the same utterance, linked by a drop-set separator. Preserve that relationship in your parsed representation.

4. Parse alternatives as competing hypotheses

Because Chrome can return up to three transcripts for one result, use the alternatives as additional evidence rather than treating the first transcript as ground truth. The Web Speech API exposes each alternative's transcript and a confidence value, but that value should not be treated as a calibrated probability that your final gym entry is correct.

For example, suppose the recognizer returns:

  • 5 kgs for 2 rapes

  • 5 kgs for 2 reps

  • 5 kgs for 2 rips

All three can map to the same structured interpretation:

5 kg × 2 reps

That is stronger evidence than a single transcript containing 5 kgs for 2 rapes.

But consider these alternatives:

  • 5 kg for 2 reps

  • 5 kg for 4 reps

These represent genuinely different workout entries. You must not merge them into one result simply because their text is similar.

My recommended candidate-scoring strategy

Generate several plausible parses from each transcript, apply your contextual normalization rules, and score the resulting structured entries.

An initial, hand-tuned scoring function might be:

Plain text
score = 5 × recognized_weight + 5 × recognized_rep_count + 3 × valid_set_structure + 3 × agreement_with_other_alternatives + 2 × valid_unit - 4 × unsupported_insertions - 5 × conflicting_quantities

These numbers are illustrative weights, not statistically validated probabilities. Tune them against your own labeled recordings.

More importantly, don't reward a candidate simply because it has the most fields. A hallucinated rep count should never beat a partially parsed but faithful result.

Use the best-scoring candidate only when it wins clearly. If two candidates differ in weight or reps and their scores are close, flag the field for confirmation.

One implementation detail: don't combine individual words across alternatives as though they were independent recognitions. Each alternative is a complete hypothesis for the utterance. Parse each one, then compare their structured outputs.

5. A concrete JavaScript implementation

Here's how I'd implement the core normalizer in plain JavaScript, without dependencies or a build step.

The important design choice is that the normalizer emits candidate interpretations, not irreversible replacements. The first version below covers the recurring ASR errors you reported; it is deliberately not the entire workout parser.

JavaScript

const REP_ALIASES = new Set([
  "raps", "rips", "ribs", "rapes", "wraps",
  "grapes", "tips", "apps"
]);

const WEIGHT_UNITS = new Set([
  "kg", "kgs", "kilogram", "kilograms",
  "lb", "lbs", "pound", "pounds"
]);

function tokenize(text) {
  return text
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[’']/g, "")
    .replace(/[.,!?;:]/g, " ")
    .replace(/\b(\d+)(st|nd|rd|th)\b/g, "$1")
    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
    .trim()
    .split(" ")
    .filter(Boolean);
}

// Produce normalized tokens while retaining a trace of rewrites.
// Contextual rules are intentionally conservative.
function normalizeTokens(tokens) {
  const out = [];
  const trace = [];

  function emit(value, original, rule) {
    out.push(value);
    if (rule) {
      trace.push({ original, replacement: value, rule });
    }
  }

  for (let i = 0; i < tokens.length; i++) {
    const token = tokens[i];
    const next = tokens[i + 1];
    const next2 = tokens[i + 2];
    const prev = out[out.length - 1];

    // "20 kgs" and "20 kg is" use the same unit.
    if (
      token === "is" &&
      WEIGHT_UNITS.has(prev)
    ) {
      trace.push({
        original: "is",
        replacement: "",
        rule: "unit-is-artifact"
      });
      continue;
    }

    // "for 20" can be transcribed as "420".
    // Only split when a preceding weight and a set
    // continuation make the interpretation plausible.
    if (
      /^\d{2,3}$/.test(token) &&
      /^(20|25|30|40|50|60|70|80|90|100|120)$/.test(token) &&
      prev === "kg" &&
      false
    ) {
      // Intentionally disabled in this generic pass.
      // Implement "420" handling in the set grammar,
      // where the preceding set and expected field are known.
    }

    // "20 grapes", "10 rips", etc.
    if (
      REP_ALIASES.has(token) &&
      /^\d+$/.test(prev || "")
    ) {
      emit("reps", token, "contextual-rep-alias");
      continue;
    }

    // Keep "g" for the grammar to interpret.
    // It is too ambiguous for a global rewrite.
    emit(token, token, null);
  }

  return { tokens: out, trace };
}

This is intentionally a starting point, not a complete parser. In particular, 420, to enter, and 4 need to be resolved within a set's expected fields, not in this generic token pass.

I would also store a normalized transcript and a list of applied rewrite rules. That will make it much easier to investigate why a particular recording became a particular entry.

6. Interim transcripts need a separate policy

Your logs show why interim results must not be treated like final commands:

20 kgs for 10 ra → 20 kgs for 10 rap → 20 kgs for 10 grapes

The recognizer is revising its hypothesis, not issuing three separate commands. The Web Speech API explicitly allows interim results to be overwritten by subsequent results.

MDN
+1

I'd use these rules:

  • Interim: update a live preview, but never commit a set.

  • Final: parse the complete final transcript and its alternatives.

  • Incomplete command: show the recognized fields and leave missing fields unresolved.

  • Correction: allow the user to edit a field without having to repeat the whole command.

For example, 20 kgs for 10 ra can show a provisional preview of 20 kg and a likely rep count of 10, but it should not claim the word reps has been conclusively recognized.

One additional detail: if you listen to multiple result events in a continuous session, don't simply concatenate every interim transcript. Maintain the recognizer's current result list, because interim entries can be replaced or removed.

7. Add a validation layer that understands gym commands

Normalization should not be the only source of confidence. Your app already knows what a valid gym entry looks like.

Use the following contextual rules:

Situation

Parser behavior

Weight and rep count are both clear

Accept the set

Weight is clear, reps are missing

Preserve the partial set

warm UPS follows a weight

Interpret as a warm-up flag

then separates two valid set patterns

Create a new set

drop to or dropped to separates sets

Mark the later set as a drop set

add comment starts a comment

Stop parsing set fields and capture the remainder

each side / per side occurs

Set the appropriate flag

failure, spotted, or light help occurs

Parse the support field

4 could mean either for or four reps

Compare complete parses; request correction if unresolved

For comments, preserve the text the user intended to add. You can capitalize the first letter and normalize whitespace, but avoid aggressive substitutions inside free-form notes.

For example, add comment slow and heavy should produce Slow and heavy, not a series of inferred workout flags.

8. Build a regression suite from your nine real transcripts

Before expanding the grammar, turn your examples into automated tests. Each test should compare the final structured output against the intended sets, flags, and comment.

Here are the outcomes your tests should enforce:

Test 1 — Three sets

20 kgs for 10 rips then 15 kgs for 20 raps then 30 lb is for 10 grapes

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 15 kg × 20, 30 lb × 10.

Test 2 — High rep counts

20 kgs for 10 raps then 13 kgs for 20 raps then 5 kgs for 40 rips

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 13 kg × 20, 5 kg × 40.

Test 3 — Incomplete utterance

20 tips for

Expected: incomplete command, no invented weight or rep count.

Test 4 — Number and rep word both corrupted

20 kgs for 10 ribs then 5 kg is 420 g

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 5 kg × 20, provided the contextual correction is sufficiently supported.

Test 5 — Warm-up

20 kg warm UPS

Expected: 20 kg warm-up, with no invented rep count.

Test 6 — Phrase-level correction

20 kgs for 10 raps then 5 kg is for to enter apps

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 5 kg × 20.

Test 7 — Missing connector

20 kgs for 10 ribs then 10 kg is five raps then 5 kg is 4 2 rapes

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 10 kg × 5, 5 kg × 2, assuming the final phrase-level repair wins against competing parses.

Test 8 — Mixed rep variants

20 kgs for 10 grapes then 5 kgs for two reps then 2 kg is 20 raps

Expected: 20 kg × 10, 5 kg × 2, 2 kg × 20.

Test 9 — Multi-digit counts

10 kgs for 20 wraps then 5 kg is 25 raps then 30 kg is for two reps

Expected: 10 kg × 20, 5 kg × 25, 30 kg × 2.

These are acceptance tests for your target behavior, not proof that a particular heuristic will generalize to every recording.

I'd also add negative tests, especially:

  • 20 kg for 4 reps must remain four reps, not twenty-four.

  • 5 kg for 12 reps must not turn into 5 kg × 4 × 12.

  • 20 kg must not automatically become 20 reps.

  • A comment containing slow, failure, or help must not be reinterpreted as a set field after the comment boundary.

  • 5 blocks for 10 reps must preserve machine blocks rather than convert them into a mass unit.

9. Use your own recordings to improve the rules

The fastest route to a reliable parser is to collect a small, labeled evaluation set from your actual gym environment.

For each recording, store:

  • The final transcript and all returned alternatives.

  • The intended structured workout entry.

  • Which correction rules fired.

  • Whether the parser accepted the result automatically or asked for confirmation.

  • Whether the user edited the result.

Evaluate field-level accuracy, not just whether the entire sentence parsed. Weight accuracy, rep-count accuracy, unit accuracy, set-boundary accuracy, and comment accuracy can be measured separately.

That distinction matters: a parser that gets 95% of words right can still be dangerous if its remaining errors systematically change a weight or rep count.

You can also explore contextual phrase hints in Chrome where supported. The Web Speech API documents SpeechRecognition.phrases as a way to bias recognition toward domain-specific vocabulary, although support and behavior vary by implementation. It is worth testing terms such as reps, kilograms, drop set, and your common exercise vocabulary, but don't depend on it as your primary correction mechanism.

My final recommendation

Build the parser in this order:

  1. A deterministic set grammar with explicit command boundaries.

  2. Contextual correction rules for your recurring ASR errors.

  3. Candidate parsing across the final transcript and its alternatives.

  4. Confidence and ambiguity handling at the individual-field level.

  5. A regression suite built from your real logs.

  6. Optional recognition phrase hints after the parser is already working.

The single most important implementation rule: never let a text-normalization shortcut silently change a weight or rep count when another plausible interpretation exists. Make the common errors effortless to correct, and make uncertain entries obvious.

That gives you a lightweight, maintainable parser that runs entirely in the browser, works with your current JavaScript setup, and can improve as you collect more recordings—without requiring a backend or an external AI service.
